api_field_reliability.finding: Every matching-rule claim in entry_logic.match_rule_reference checks out against the code: team normalization via a 30-team alias table (normalize_mlb_team), Eastern-calendar date via _iso_date/zoneinfo, unique-event-key rejection (match_events counts and drops ambiguous_keys where either venue has >1 candidate for a key), and a hard-coded max_start_difference_seconds=900.0 (exactly 15 minutes) that moves a match to schedule_mismatches rather than accepting it — confirmed by a passing test (test_gemini_kalshi_research.py asserts schedule_mismatches==1 for a >15min gap). Phase classification in src/dislocation_cases.py (_finish_case) uses scheduled_start = min(gemini_start, kalshi_start) — literally the 'earlier of the two venue start times' the doc and spec describe — and labels pre_scheduled_start only when the first observation timestamp precedes that scheduled_start. Critically for the CLAUDE.md gotcha: Kalshi's contribution to 'scheduled_start_at' is NOT close_time, occurrence_datetime, expiration_time, expected_expiration_time, or latest_expiration_time — grep of src/gemini_kalshi_research.py finds none of those field names anywhere. _kalshi_datetime() instead parses the date/time directly out of the KXMLBGAME event ticker string via regex (e.g. 'KXMLBGAME-26AUG021340PITCIN' -> 2026-08-02 13:40 ET), which is exactly the workaround CLAUDE.md itself prescribes ('the real game time is in the TICKER, not a field'). The spec does not misuse any Kalshi open-market time field; the collector correctly sidesteps the documented placeholder trap.

contract_terms.finding: Independently confirmed the postponement/rescheduling divergence the spec and the yaml both claim, by reading the actual rule text at both pinned URLs rather than trusting the quoted summary. Kalshi MLBGAME.pdf verbatim: postponed games remain open only if 'rescheduled and started within 48 hours of its originally scheduled start time'; otherwise 'the market will resolve based on the last fair market price as determined by the Exchange.' Gemini BASEBALL1 Rule 13.166(e)(1)(i) verbatim: 'the Contract shall remain open and active' until the rescheduled game is played, resolving only 'by the date that is the latter of (A) the final rescheduled day of the regular season ... or (B) ... the final scheduled day of the applicable postseason round or tournament stage,' i.e. a season/round-length window versus Kalshi's 48-hour window — exactly the divergence the spec's basis_risk_disclosure describes ('Gemini holds a postponed MLB market open until played or season end; Kalshi uses a shorter rescheduling window and may resolve at a fair price'). This is a genuine, verified-in-text divergence, not an inferred one. I could not independently recompute the pinned SHA-256 hashes (no shell/hashing tool available in this review), so hash-level document integrity rests on the pinned registry and its daily verification timer, not on a hash I computed myself; the document CONTENT fetched today at the same URLs is consistent with what both the yaml's rationale and the spec describe. One non-blocking nuance for the record: Gemini Rule 13.166(e)(1)(iv) resolves a tie to 'No' on both team contracts, while Kalshi's BASEBALLGAMEWIN resolves an unlisted tie to a $1/n split (each team $0.50) — a real difference in tie-handling that the yaml's 8-dimension table has no explicit 'tie_handling' row for (it would presumably fall under binary_payout, labeled 'equivalent'). This is low-materiality (MLB games are essentially never officially recorded as ties; extra innings are played to a decision) and the spec makes no claim resting on tie-payout equivalence, so it does not affect this spec's verified claims, but it is a gap in the yaml's dimension coverage worth a future reviewer's attention.

external_schedule_dependency.detail: The spec's live gating logic (entry_logic preconditions 1-6, phase classification) depends only on each venue's own self-reported/embedded scheduled-start data — Gemini's event 'startTime' field and Kalshi's date/time embedded in the KXMLBGAME event ticker string — neither of which is an external data feed; both are read directly from the venues being collected. This is a materially different situation from P-022's ESPN golf-schedule dependency, where Kalshi's own OPEN-market fields are placeholders with no usable value at all, forcing reliance on an outside source. Here, the ticker substring is assigned at listing time and is not subject to the close_time-rewrite behavior CLAUDE.md documents. A genuinely external MLB schedule IS used elsewhere in the pipeline (research/GEMINI_KALSHI_READ_ONLY_RESEARCH.md describes a separate 'crossvenue-settlement-evidence.timer' / settlement_basis_evidence.json that joins cases to public MLB schedule outcomes to measure historical postponement/suspension incidence), but that module is explicitly a diagnostic/evidence artifact for measuring incidence after the fact ('historical incidence remains explicitly unmeasured until event-outcome evidence is joined') — it is not cited anywhere in the spec's entry_logic preconditions and does not gate any decision this spec makes. Available=true is reported as not-applicable-but-non-blocking since nothing in the spec requires it.
external_schedule_dependency.extra_note: Confirmed absent: the spec references no field named 'schedule' or external calendar anywhere in preconditions 1-6; only 'scheduled starts agree within 15 minutes' (both venue-native fields).

extra.verdict_rationale: This spec correctly and verifiably describes a strategy that is currently, and correctly, gated to zero risk. Every checkable factual claim — the postponement/rescheduling divergence, the settlement-equivalence state machine and its code-level enforcement, both venues' fee formulas and independent per-leg rounding, and the matching/phase-classification mechanics including the deliberate avoidance of Kalshi's open-market close_time placeholder trap — was verified against primary sources (live-fetched rule PDFs read verbatim, live-fetched fee page, and direct reads of the actual collector/registry code and its tests), not against the spec's or card's own quoted summaries. A correct description of a blocked strategy is a pass, per this review's charter.
